{
  "need": "Competence",
  "secondary": { "name": "Status" },
  "read": "Tears after correction usually signal that this student has tied their worth to their output — a stumble on the work feels like a verdict on them as a person. The status angle: if they believe you see them as less capable when they make mistakes, the feedback feels like a demotion, not guidance.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Soften or skip the hard feedback to stop the tears — but that robs the student of the honest input they need to actually grow, and quietly signals you don't believe they can handle the truth." },
  "mentorMove": "Separate the person from the draft: make clear the feedback is aimed at the work because the work can get better, not because the student is lacking. Deliver the high standard alongside a genuine statement of belief in their ability to reach it.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "Give the real feedback every time — watered-down notes are a kindness that quietly communicates low expectations.",
    "Keep the standard visible: name what excellent looks like and hold that line even when the conversation gets emotional."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "Adjust the delivery mode — written comments first so they can absorb privately before a short conversation, or a two-sentence verbal heads-up before the marked work lands.",
    "Let them choose when to talk it through — 'read it over and come find me when you're ready' hands them some control over the moment."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 1, "label": "Empathy" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, before you look at my notes — I want to say something first. I push on your work because I think it matters, and because I think you can do more with it. That's the only reason any of this is on there." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "When you get feedback, what does it feel like in the moment? Is it the specific comments, or is it more like a general 'ugh, I messed up' feeling?" },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here's what I want to try: I'll always tell you one thing that's genuinely working before I get into what needs fixing — not to soften it, but because both things are real. And if you need a minute before we talk, take it. Deal?" },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I'm going to keep giving you honest feedback because I hold you to a high standard and I genuinely believe you can get there. A hard note on a draft just means the draft isn't finished yet — it says nothing about you." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Over time, help this student build a mental separation between 'my work needs revision' and 'I am not good enough' — that shift is the real skill. Name it explicitly when you see them recover and use feedback well: 'That right there, taking a hard note and running with it, that's what strong writers do.'"
}
situation: A sensitive student tears up whenever I correct their work, and I find myself softening real feedback to avoid it.
